paragraphs.text: Yesterday, lovers of Christ, we sang the praises of the coming of the holy and adorable Spirit. That coming is not honored by human notions; it is attested by the Father's power. For the word of God is not established by what we reason or utter, but by what enlightens us, and by this piety is established and the truth proclaimed. The word of God alone, the teaching of the Holy Spirit alone, is the lamp of piety, the proclamation of the knowledge of God, and the illumination of divine teaching. So we must dwell further on the explanation of the holy and adorable Spirit, and say something clearer about that holy and glorious Power. To use the same words again: the Holy Spirit is indivisible in nature, since he proceeded from the indivisible and undivided nature. This is what the divine words teach, or rather what the Spirit proclaims about himself, speaking through the prophets and shedding his own ray through the apostles.

His name is Holy Spirit, Spirit of truth, Spirit of God, Spirit of the Lord, Spirit of the Father, Spirit of the Son, Spirit of Christ. This is what Scripture calls him, or rather what he calls himself: both Spirit of God and the Spirit who is from God. When we hear "Spirit of God," we might think he is called this only because he belongs to God. To prevent that, Scripture brings in the Holy Spirit and adds "from God" to "of God." "Of God" is one thing and "from God" another. Heaven and earth are "of God," since he made them. But nothing is said to be "from God" unless it is from his essence. So he is called Holy Spirit. This is his proper and primary title, the one with the most expressive meaning, which shows the nature of the Holy Spirit. Holy Spirit, Spirit of God. Who calls him Spirit of God? Listen to the Savior: "But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God." Spirit of God. As I said before, someone hearing "Spirit of God" might think it means mere belonging and not a sharing of nature. To prevent that, Paul says: "But you have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God." Again, he is called Spirit of the Father, as the Savior tells the apostles: "Do not worry about how or what you will say; for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of our Father who speaks in you." Scripture said "Spirit of God" and then added "from God." In the same way, he is again called Spirit of the Father. And in case you think this is said only because he belongs to the Father, the Savior confirms it: "But when the Advocate comes, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father." There it was "from God," here it is "from the Father." He said of himself, "I came forth from the Father," and he said of the Holy Spirit, "who proceeds from the Father." So he is the Spirit of God and the Spirit of God the Father, and he proceeds from the Father. What does "proceeds" mean? He did not say "is begotten," and we must not think what is not written. The Son is begotten of the Father; the Spirit proceeds from the Father.

No doubt you want me to explain the difference: How was the one begotten? How did the other proceed? Well then: because you have learned that he was begotten, have you also learned how? Because you hear the Son proclaimed, have you grasped how he was begotten? These are names honored by faith and guarded by pious reasoning. So what is the force of "proceeds"? Scripture wants to avoid the word "begetting," so that it does not call him a son. So it says "Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father." It presents him as proceeding, like water gushing from the earth, as was said of paradise: "A river proceeds out of Eden." He proceeds and wells up. The Father is called a fountain of living water, as the prophet Jeremiah says: "Heaven was astonished at this, and the earth shuddered greatly, for my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water." By defining him as the fountain of living water, the divine word presented the Father as the fountain of life, from which the living water proceeds. "Who proceeds from the Father." What proceeds? The Holy Spirit. How? As water from a fountain. How do we know that the Holy Spirit is called water? The Savior says: "Whoever believes in me, as Scripture has said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water." And the evangelist explains this water, adding: "He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive." The evangelist John, then, made it plain that the living water is the Holy Spirit. And the Father says, "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water." So the Father is the fountain of the Spirit. That is why the Spirit proceeds from the Father. So he is called (I repeat it) Spirit of God and Spirit from God, Spirit of the Father and Spirit from the Father. Isaiah bears witness to the name "Spirit of the Lord," speaking in the person of Christ: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me." And Paul says: "Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom." If there is freedom wherever the Spirit comes, is he himself a slave? The Holy Spirit breaks the yoke of slavery for those he visits and grants them the standing of free people. How then can he be a slave? How can he give what he does not have? How can he set others free if he is a slave? Have you not heard Paul say: "For the law of the Spirit of life has set me free in Christ Jesus"? Does the Spirit set slaves free while not being free by nature himself? If he were created and enslaved, he could not set anyone free.

Do not let heretics outwit you. I do not call him a slave or a creature; that is a new heresy. They are in danger of introducing three first principles: one uncreated, one created, and a third I do not know what to call. Spirit of God, Spirit from God, Spirit of the Father, Spirit who proceeds from the Father, Spirit of the Lord, Spirit of the Son. The apostle says: "And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, 'Abba, Father.'" There is the Spirit of the Son. Elsewhere Paul again speaks of the Spirit of Christ: "But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of Christ dwells in you." Please notice this holy interweaving. Paul has laid out a kind of holy and living chain of threefold power. He binds together the indivisible nature and shows one power under different names: "But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit." There is "Spirit." "If indeed the Spirit of Christ dwells in you." There is "Spirit of God" [?]. "But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ." Surely he ought to have said, "But if anyone does not have the Spirit of God." Yet he said "Spirit of Christ." He said "Spirit of God" and then added "the Spirit of Christ." "But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him." He said this to show that where the Spirit is, Christ is too. For Christ to be present is the same as for the Spirit to be present, and to say "Spirit of God" is the same as to say "Spirit of Christ." So he is the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of truth, which is as much as to say the Spirit of the Son, since the Savior says: "I am the truth." He is called the Spirit of truth, which means the Spirit of the Son, as Paul says: "God has sent the Spirit of his Son." So he is both the Spirit of the Son and the Spirit of him who raised Jesus Christ. Listen to Paul himself: "But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus Christ dwells in you." These are the names of that holy and spotless Power, the holy and adorable Spirit. But there are other names too, which belong not to his nature but to his activity. The subject is deep and needs attentive, careful and faithful listening. The Spirit is also called Spirit of life, since the Savior says: "I am the truth and the life." He is called Spirit of life, as Paul also says: "For the law of the Spirit of life." These names belong to his very sovereignty, his very nature. But there are other names that are given not to the Holy Spirit himself but to his power and activity, such as his gifts. I will state the idea, make it clearer, and bring in the evidence. Suppose the Holy Spirit, through the prayers of the saints, grants sanctification to me or to another Christian. I receive a gift, so that my body and soul are holy. The gift given to me is called a spirit of holiness, that is, a grace-gift. Suppose the Holy Spirit gives someone a gift without wisdom or knowledge, giving him faith alone. There are many like this, with the gift of believing the Scriptures: they do not know the Scriptures, yet they believe them. That gift is called a spirit of faith. If someone receives from the Holy Spirit the power and gift to believe the promise of the good things that will be given in the age to come, he has received a spirit of promise. If someone receives the gift of wisdom, the gift is called a spirit of wisdom. Everywhere the gifts of the Spirit are called "spirit." Pay close attention, for we are explaining these insights only in part and in outline. Now let us come to the proofs. When someone has the gift of love, he is said to have a spirit of love. When someone receives the gift of martyrdom, he is said to have a spirit of power, that is, a grace-gift. Since the giver is the Holy Spirit, the gift, the grace, is called by the same name. That is why Paul says: "For you did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you received a spirit of adoption." And again: "For he did not give us a spirit of cowardice, but a spirit of power and love and self-discipline." Here he uses "spirit" to mean the gift, as when he says: "You were sealed with the holy Spirit of promise." Where is "spirit of promise" written? Paul says: "Having the same spirit of faith and of promise," that is, the gift of the Spirit. So there you have a spirit of faith and a spirit of promise. If someone is gentle and humble of heart, he has received a gift of gentleness, and it is a grace-gift of God. Paul says this too: "If a person is caught in some transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness," that is, in the grace of the gift of gentleness. "Look to yourself," he says, "so that you too are not tempted." There is a spirit of gentleness. To another is given sanctification of soul and body, and this is called a spirit of holiness, as he says: "Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his prophets, according to the spirit of holiness." He has put it in inverted order. The sense is this: Paul, who became an apostle according to the spirit of holiness. Many followed the first wording and took it to mean "who was designated Son of God according to the spirit of holiness." But that is not the meaning. Rather, it means: Paul, appointed an apostle according to the spirit of holiness. And when was he appointed? "From the resurrection of Jesus Christ." The other apostles were appointed before the Passion; he was appointed after the resurrection. Hence "according to the spirit of holiness." I will add something else. When we all begin to say, at the hour of the mysteries, "Our Father, who art in heaven," we have received a gift, the spirit of adoption, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit. It is also called a spirit of zeal, as Paul says: "Since you too are zealous for spirits," that is, you are eager for spiritual gifts. "Since you are zealous for spirits," that is, for the gifts. "And I will show you a still more excellent way. If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am nothing." That is, love is greater than every gift.

But let us return to our subject. Here Isaiah comes in again, for the same Spirit speaks through them all. Paul spoke of a spirit of life, a spirit of love, a spirit of power, a spirit of self-discipline, a spirit of promise, a spirit of faith, a spirit of gentleness, a spirit of adoption. In the same way blessed Isaiah says: "A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse," meaning the Savior's royal rod. He calls the royal emblem a rod, as David says: "A rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom." "A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up from it, and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him."

Here is the name of the Spirit's own nature. Then come the gifts: "a spirit of wisdom and understanding, a spirit of counsel and might, a spirit of knowledge, a spirit of piety, a spirit of the fear of God." Take an example. You, a believer, or some other Christian, open a passage of Scripture with a hidden and obscure meaning. The Holy Spirit grants that the hidden meanings be revealed. That is a gift that reveals the depths. This is why the apostle, wanting the disciples of piety to understand the Scriptures, says: "I pray to God that he may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in knowledge, the eyes of your mind being enlightened." Do you see the spirit of revelation? But let us return to our subject. Where one must learn the depths, it is called a spirit of revelation. Where one must have love, it is called a spirit of love. Where the teacher must speak clearly, it is called a spirit of wisdom. Where the hearer must understand intelligently, it is called a spirit of understanding. The spirit of wisdom is given to those who teach, the spirit of understanding to those who listen. I preach; you know how to understand but not how to teach. The gift of wisdom is so called because it teaches. God sends the teacher a word of wisdom, and in the same way he sends the learner a gift of understanding, so that the learner may understand the things of God. To show this, he says: "The preaching mouth has the grace of wisdom; the learning heart has the grace of understanding." Wisdom is the weapon of the mouth; understanding is the weapon of the heart. That is why David says: "My mouth shall speak wisdom, and the meditation of my heart understanding." Another person did not receive the grace of teaching, but received the grace to give good and admirable advice and counsel. Sometimes the teacher does not know how to give advice, because he did not receive that gift. No one receives everything, so that no one may think grace is a matter of nature. One receives the grace of teaching, and so that he is not puffed up, he finds himself weak when it comes to counsel in practical affairs. Another cannot teach, but gives good counsel. So the one who lends to others finds himself borrowing elsewhere. Where can we see this? I will now show you that one who has received the grace of teaching needs someone else's advice. Moses received a spirit of wisdom, of lawgiving, of teaching, and he took it upon himself to judge the people all day long. Then Jethro his father-in-law comes and advises him: "You cannot judge so great a people alone. You will wear yourself out completely if you do this. What should you do? Appoint leaders of tens and of fifties and of hundreds and of thousands. Then the leader of ten can refer to the leader of fifty whatever is beyond him. The leader of fifty can refer to the leader of a thousand whatever is beyond him. The leader of a thousand can refer to you whatever is beyond him. And whatever is beyond you, you will refer to God." "If there is any difficult matter," he says, "they will bring it to you; and if anything is too hard for you, you will bring it to God." And the lawgiver, wise as he was, accepted a layman's advice. That advice became law and an image of things to come. Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, had been a priest of idols. Later he rejected that error, learned the truth, and became an image of the Church of the Gentiles. He shows that the understanding of the Gentiles surpasses the wisdom of the Law, not because they are Gentiles but because they have repented. For when was Jethro's advice accepted? Not while he was a priest, but after he had come to know God. When he saw God's works and Moses told him of the wonders in Egypt, he said: "Now I know" (see his repentance) "that the Lord your God is great above all gods." So from the moment he knew the truth, he received the gift of good counsel.

But let us return to our subject. The one who teaches received a spirit of wisdom, and the one who is taught a spirit of understanding, so that he may understand. That is why Isaiah ascribes wisdom to the one who speaks and understanding to the one who listens, saying: "A wise master builder and an understanding hearer." A spirit of counsel is given to the one who gives advice, and a spirit of might to the one who receives the advice. The adviser receives grace to say something good; the one who receives the advice receives grace to carry out what is beneficial. A spirit of the fear of God. Each of these gifts was given for the need at hand. Indeed, when the tabernacle was being built under Moses in the wilderness, there was no need there for a gift of teaching. What was needed was a gift of craftsmanship: how to weave the fine linen, the blue, the scarlet, the purple. God gave the grace of a gift of craftsmanship, of weaving, of loom-work, of goldsmithing, of stone-cutting, of embroidery. And why did he give these crafts? Because God was making the tabernacle on earth. The tabernacle was an image of heaven and earth, and God made heaven and earth in six days. The tabernacle was being built as a figure of heaven and earth, and there was need of a gift of the Holy Spirit suited to the task. It was not a time for teaching but for weaving and the other crafts. And God says: "See, I have called by name Bezalel of the tribe of Judah, and I have filled him with a divine spirit, a spirit of wisdom and knowledge and perception." Wisdom, to instruct the workers to work in such a way or to make this or that. Knowledge, so that he might fit things together. Perception, so that he might grasp the meaning of the things God spoke. Elsewhere God promises to give a grace of loving-kindness, and says: "I will pour out on the house of David a spirit of grace and compassion," that is, a gift of loving-kindness. Again, he bestows a gift of humility. Where do we find this? The three young men in the furnace. As righteous men they trampled the flame, but as humble men they called themselves sinners. Through their surpassing righteousness they trampled the flame and turned the furnace into dew. Yet they were not puffed up, and they did not say: "Oh, how righteousness is with us! We have conquered nature; we have gone beyond law." Instead they act as righteous men and speak as sinners. Just think: they were trampling the flame and dancing as saints, and confessing as sinners: "We have sinned, we have done lawlessly, we have done wrong. All that you have brought upon us you have done in true judgment, for we acted lawlessly in departing from you, and we did not listen to your commandments, that it might go well with us." Since, then, though they were righteous, they humbled themselves, they received a spirit of humiliation, a gift of humility. That is why, seeing the grace, they say that at this time we have no prophet, no offering, no incense, no place to make an offering and find mercy. Since, then, we have no city, no temple, no altar, no incense, humility will be enough for us in place of them all. That is why they say: "But with a contrite soul and a spirit of humility may we be accepted." Of another, when he is full of grace and has received the gift entire, it is said: he received a spirit of fullness. Where do we find this? Jeremiah says: "The way of the daughter of my people is not toward the holy, nor toward the pure, a spirit of fullness." They do not have, he says, the spirit that fills them. In this way the apostles had a spirit of fullness, as it is written: "Then Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit," when he rebukes Elymas the sorcerer. Do you see the gifts? I repeat, then, the names of the ineffable nature: Spirit of God, Spirit that is from God, Spirit of the Lord, Spirit of the Father, Spirit of the Son, Spirit of Christ, Spirit of him who raised Christ, Spirit of life, Spirit of truth. Next, the gifts: spirit of power, spirit of love, spirit of self-control, spirit of promise, spirit of faith, spirit of revelation, spirit of adoption. When someone receives the gift of judging, he has received a spirit of judgment, as Isaiah says: "And the Lord will cleanse them by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning." He calls the punishing and cleansing power a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning. David asks for a right spirit, the one that leads to uprightness. And again he asks for a gift that governs the passions and keeps the soul from being enslaved to them. David's heart had been perverted, and he had fallen from self-control into the vice of passion and pleasure. He had unjustly decided that the man should be killed, had become a slave of desire and had turned to adultery. So he asks for a right spirit, saying: "Renew within me, and do not cast me away from your presence; restore to me the joy of your salvation and uphold me with a governing spirit," that is, with a gift that governs the passions and masters the pleasures.

This is what we have said about the divine authority of the Holy Spirit and about the differences among his works. But the heretics do not know that when Scripture says "spirit of holiness" or "of promise," it is speaking of the gifts. They apply these phrases to the nature, saying that God gave the Holy Spirit and bestowed him. "Do you see," they say, "that he is a gift of God?" They read what concerns the gifts and applied it to the nature, when they ought to have understood which names indicate the nature and which names express the grace. They have peddled the truth, confused everything, overturned themselves, run aground away from the truth. "Their senseless heart was darkened; claiming to be wise, they became fools." So they go on: "Since," one of them says, "you raise questions about the Spirit and teach from the Scriptures, and want the Scriptures as your witnesses, we too start from these same Scriptures and cite what the Savior said about the Holy Spirit. What then does he say? 'When the Paraclete comes, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will guide you into all the truth; for he will not speak on his own, but whatever he hears he will declare to you; for he will take from what is mine and declare it to you.' Do you see," he says, "how he does not speak on his own, but takes from him? How can the Spirit's authority possibly be demonstrated? Has not Scripture shown," he says, "that he is subject to the Son's authority, borrowing from him and supplying others?" Pay close attention. When something that is said seems puzzling to you, do not pounce at once on the word, but wait for the thought to be completed. Have you not seen, when materials are being prepared for buildings, how everything lies jumbled together: lime, stones, timber? To your eyes everything is in confusion, but to the craftsman everything has its place. He knows the moment when this jumbled piece will fit that one, and that one this. And the scattered pieces, once they receive their proper arrangement, produce the beauty of the building. So when you see the speaker passing from this to that, and from that to something else, understand that he is preparing his materials. For once I have laid out the materials, then I show how they fit together. The Son and the Spirit have one nature, one power, one truth, one life, one wisdom. But from the time the Savior deigned to take on our created form, he is filled with the Holy Spirit. This is not because he is lower than the Holy Spirit, but because the flesh had to receive the coming of the Spirit in human fashion. It is not that God the Word could not sanctify the created form he had assumed. For if you go down that line of reasoning, the Son too is superfluous, since the Father would have been enough to sanctify the created form. Does the Father take the Son as his helper because he is weak? Does the Son take the Spirit as his helper because he is weak? No. Since it is one nature that works all things in all, some things the Father does and they are counted as the work of the whole nature; some the Son does and they extend to the whole nature; some the Spirit does and they are credited to the whole nature. When the nature is considered in itself, it is equal and uniform, full of sovereign authority, marvelous, neither lacking nor incomplete, not advancing, not diminishing, not lessened, not receiving additions. But when God the Word assumes the flesh taken from us, he makes it receive the Holy Spirit in human fashion, like one of the prophets or one of the apostles. I said it in advance: this is not as though the Son's divinity were insufficient, but so that the knowledge of the Trinity might be shown complete in this created form. The Lord's flesh, then, was deemed worthy of the Holy Spirit. And from then on the Savior wished to make the created form he had assumed the Holy Spirit's own, so that whatever Christ did according to the flesh would be ascribed to the Holy Spirit who dwelt in him as in a holy human temple. For he is man for our sake, but God in his own right: God in his own right, man out of love for humankind. He cast out demons and chose to ascribe the expulsion of the demons to the Holy Spirit, saying: "But if I cast out demons by the Holy Spirit." He did not say "by God the Word," but ascribes it to the Holy Spirit, as a holy man deemed worthy of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, when he went into the temple, he takes the prophet Isaiah and reads. And he reads what was written about himself. "And having unrolled the book," it says, he reads: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me." Does this fit God the Word? Does God say, "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me"? Is it not beyond dispute that it is the man who speaks? "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me." I was anointed, he says, by the Holy Spirit. That is why Peter says: "Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power."

Let us keep our minds on this, I beg you. For all this is preparation for "he will take from what is mine." We have not been drifting from one thing to another. As I said before, I am getting the materials ready so that you may fit them together. He was deemed worthy of the Holy Spirit. He was baptized in the Jordan, and John says: "I saw the heavens opened and the Spirit of God descending like a dove and remaining on him." Do you see how he receives the Holy Spirit in human fashion? No one is so impious as to think that the Godhead received the Spirit. John the Baptist says: "Among you stands one whom you do not know, and I did not know him; but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me, 'The one on whom you see the Holy Spirit descending like a dove and remaining on him, this is my Son.'" The Holy Spirit came down so that Isaiah's words might be fulfilled: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me." The flesh was baptized, and as soon as he was baptized he came up from the water and was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness. He was led up, and the flesh had the Holy Spirit as its guide. Why was he led? To give you a pattern: "Just as my flesh is not led by desires but is led by the Spirit, so you too ought to be." That is why Paul too says: "But if you are led by the Spirit of God, you are no longer in the flesh," and "All who are led by the Spirit of God are not under law." Christ's flesh is led; let us be led too. This is why he takes everything upon himself: to leave us a pattern. He was led up by the Spirit to be tempted, and he conquered the devil. It was not the Godhead that conquered, for it would be an insult to the Godhead to say, "I conquered." God is never defeated, nor does he conquer; he always rules. If he can win a victory, then surely he could also be defeated. But he who always rules is the Almighty. Those he rules do not rebel against him, and he does not prevail over his subjects by toil. If, then, the Lord's flesh, the Lord's created form, the extraordinary man, the heavenly one, the new shoot that blossomed from an extraordinary birth, receives the Holy Spirit, you have the testimonies that the Spirit came from heaven, and that the Spirit led him up to overcome the devil. The image of Adam, which had been led astray in the beginning, was now to win. So the extraordinary man went in, escorted by the power of the Spirit. That is why, just as Scripture said, "He was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted," so when he returned as victor, it says: "And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit from the wilderness." So the flesh had the Holy Spirit. It did not have a portion of the gifts as we do, wisdom to one and knowledge to another, but it had all the gifts. Truly I am anxious and tremble lest the weakness of my tongue blunt the greatness of what is being proclaimed. So the Lord's body, the holy flesh, when it received the working of the Holy Spirit, did not receive one or two graces, as the apostles and prophets did. For a human being cannot contain everything. That is why Paul says: "Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Do all have gifts of healing?" Among us the gifts are divided. But in Christ's flesh were all the graces, all the gifts, according to the substance of the flesh. And pay attention. He first filled his own temple with every grace. He had the gift of healing diseases, casting out demons, raising the dead, prophesying, doing the works of truth. He could do everything and had the fullness of the gifts, from the time the Lord's flesh was filled with all the gifts. And we certainly needed to receive in part, as from a reservoir. From the Lord's body, from him, the gifts are supplied to apostles and prophets. John testified that in him is the whole fullness of the Godhead, and Paul says: "In whom the whole fullness of the Godhead dwelt bodily." He did not simply say, "In whom the Godhead dwelt," but "the fullness of the Godhead," that is, every gift of the Godhead.

And so that no one might think it dwelt in God the Word, he says: "In whom the whole fullness of the Godhead dwelt bodily." In his flesh was the whole fullness of wisdom, understanding, power, signs, every kind of working. From that fullness, then, we all borrow. John the Baptist testifies: "I did not know him, but he who sent me to baptize said to me, 'The one on whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining' (he did not say "granting him one gift," but "remaining" in his entirety) 'this is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit and fire.'" Then John, wanting to show that the Savior did not receive grace as a mere man does, says: "God does not give the Spirit by measure; the Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand." Where, then, do we receive from? "From his fullness we have all received." He is the fullness; we receive from the fullness. How? From the time he filled the Lord's flesh, he drew from it as from a spring and lent the gift to human beings. Pay attention, I beg you. So he says: "When the Paraclete comes, the Spirit of truth, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will take from what is mine."

Notice how exact he is. He did not say "from me" but "from what is mine." "From me": from whom? "He will give you from what is mine"; or rather, "he will take." He takes, but not by borrowing. Since he filled the spring as the source of the gifts, he draws from the reservoir and supplies everyone from what is his own. And how do we know that to take in this way is to take from one's own? Listen. God filled Moses with the Spirit, and Moses says, "I cannot carry the burden of this people alone; appoint someone else for yourself." God says to him, "Choose seventy elders, and I will take some of the Spirit that is on you and put it on them." He did not say, "I will take what is yours," but "some of the Spirit that is on you": in other words, "I will take from what is mine." God says, "In those days I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and they shall prophesy." If God borrowed when he took from Moses, then the Spirit also borrowed when he took from the Son. For Moses was a type of Christ. Just as the seventy came from Moses, so the whole world received the Holy Spirit from Christ. "He will take from what is mine": from what he supplied to me alone, the Lord's own humanity, he will take. He is the very one who gave, who came and remained on me, who anointed me, who sanctified me, who led me into the wilderness and brought me back as victor. "He will take from what is mine and declare it to you." He was speaking not of the Holy Spirit himself but of the gifts. To show this, right after saying "He will take from what is mine," he adds, "All that the Father has is mine." I received these things from the Holy Spirit; that is why I said, "He will take from what is mine." God sanctified the flesh by the Holy Spirit. The Father sent the gift of the Spirit into the flesh of Christ, and when grace came, it placed all its gifts in Christ. Therefore he says, "He will take from what is mine and declare it to you." What, then, is meant by "He will not speak on his own, but whatever he hears he will make known to you"? As was said before, the Holy Spirit is one thing and the gift is another, just as the king is one thing and the king's gift another. Someone at war with many different barbarian nations is at a loss where to begin. If he concentrates the war on these, another wing rises against him. If he divides himself in two, his forces are split. We stand in the middle, between the Arians, who reject the glory of Christ, and the Macedonians, who insult the divine glory of the Spirit. If I treat what concerns the Son as agreed, as I would with Macedonians, the Arian immediately attacks: "Have you convinced me about the Son, that you now talk to me about the Spirit?"

But today our subject is the Holy Spirit. Many times, by the grace given by Christ, we have won the argument about the Son, and you are witnesses that what was said then was not clever sophistry but proof from Scripture. I would have liked to build up the argument about the Son now as well, for its power always shines out from within it. But for the sake of convincing the heretics who limp concerning the Spirit, I pass over it for the present. Yet it is impossible for someone who limps concerning the Spirit to walk straight concerning the Son. To this day you cannot persuade a single Macedonian to sign the homoousion of Nicaea. They keep saying, "We hold to that faith," because nothing was spelled out there about the Spirit; at that time there was no contest or war over it. All the same, to convince them I say: it is written, "He will not speak on his own." Tell the Macedonian that this is written of the Son too. Or rather, he says it about himself: "I do not speak on my own." Pay attention, I beg you. I am drawing my evidence from what you yourself confess. With the Arian I would have to argue over "I do not speak on my own," just as over what is said about the Spirit. But with you, who profess true religion, there is no need to argue. When you discuss Christ, you call him equal to God and like the Father in all things. So I have put the question to you as to one who confesses his glory. You say of the Spirit, "He will not speak on his own." The Savior says of himself, "I do not speak on my own, but what I have heard from my Father, that is what I speak." See, the Son too does not speak on his own. So far, then, they have equal honor. This is what I say to you. The Arian is at a loss over both the one and the other. What happens to the shipwrecked happens to unbelievers, as Paul says: "who have made shipwreck of their faith." The Arians have been shipwrecked and have lost both the glory of Christ and the power of the Holy Spirit. The Macedonians are struggling to climb aboard, but they have lost half the cargo. As Paul says, "Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him." Pay attention, then, so that we do not seem to be attacking for the sake of the fight or making our case insultingly. "I do not speak on my own." Explain to me what "I do not speak on my own" means. In what sense did the Savior say it? Whatever solution the Macedonian proposes for the Son, let him apply the same to the Holy Spirit. The two stand evenly balanced: neither the Spirit nor the Son speaks on his own. The Son needs the Father, and the Spirit also needs the Father. So far, equal honor. Pay attention, then. I know I have launched out into the deep, as the power of Christ, which searches all things, has seen. I tremble more than I speak, for fear that the ship may run into a boundless abyss and there be no wind. Suppose the ship is ready, with the helmsman, the sailors, the ropes, the anchors, everything prepared, and there is no breath of wind anywhere. Does not all that equipment lie idle when the wind is not at work? That is how it is. There may be breadth of speech, depth of thought, fine phrasing and fine ideas, but if the Holy Spirit is not present to supply them, it all lies idle.

Why, then, did he say of himself, as he also said of the Spirit, "I do not speak on my own"? We have put our opponent to shame in debate. Now let us convince ourselves, and them too, if indeed they will be persuaded. We would by no means force them, but let us speak in case they may be persuaded. And do not be surprised that I, a mere man, speak this way. God says to Ezekiel, "Go to the house of Israel and speak to them; perhaps they will listen, perhaps they will believe." We say these things: perhaps they will listen, perhaps they will believe, perhaps they will agree. But if they do not agree after hearing them, we are guiltless. This is how Paul taught, and after teaching he says, "I testify to you all that I am innocent of the blood of all of you, for I did not shrink from declaring to you the way of God." And now I ask: why did the Savior say "I do not speak on my own," and of the Spirit, "He will not speak on his own"? I appeal to your love: let us fix our minds on this. Although there is one Christ, many false christs came forward, as the Savior said: "Many false christs and false prophets will come in my name." There is one Christ, whose coming was promised through the prophets, but before his coming certain deceivers appeared, saying, "We are he." Theudas says, "I am he"; Judas the Galilean says, "I am he"; and they led many astray. When the Savior came, he said, "All who came before me were thieves and robbers." Those earlier ones were deceivers who put on the name of Christ and tried hard to persuade the people that they were the Christ. They did not appear together, but each on his own, one at one time and another at another. Therefore Christ says, "All who came before me were thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them. My sheep hear my voice; they know my voice and follow me." Those false christs came, then, but did not teach from the law or from the prophets. They spoke from themselves, out of their own opinion. When the Savior came, he did not depart from the law or from the prophets. Rather, he would say, for example, "Isaiah spoke well," and again, "Is it not written in your law?" And when the devil approached him, he said to him, "It is written: You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone." So when Christ came in the flesh, he did not speak on his own but from the prophets. Those who came before Christ in Christ's name did not speak from the law or from the prophets; they spoke the things of error out of their own opinion. So the Savior says, "I do not speak on my own, as they did." To speak on one's own is to speak outside the law. That is how we too must speak. When you see heretics stirring up Aristotelian or Platonic arguments, say: "We do not speak on our own. What we have heard from Christ, that is what we say." And how do we know that someone who speaks on his own is a false prophet, or that speaking on one's own is the mark of a false prophet? The prophet Ezekiel says: "As I live, says the Lord, against the prophets who lead my people astray: I did not send them; they spoke on their own and utter things from their own hearts." Since the false prophets preached on their own, the Savior throws off the suspicion and says, "I do not speak on my own." How do we know that the Savior was suspected of being a deceiver? Let us establish this first. At the feast of Tabernacles the crowds were looking for Jesus and saying, "Where is he?" And there was disagreement about him. Some said, "He is a good man"; others said, "No, he is leading the crowd astray." Do you see how he was suspected of being a deceiver? Again, after the holy death of the Savior, the chief priests say to Pilate, "Sir, we know that that deceiver said while he was still alive, 'After three days I will rise.'" I have said this to show that he was thought to be a deceiver. Since he was thought to be a deceiver, he says, "I do not speak on my own": rather, I speak from the law and from the prophets, "what I have heard from the Father." It was not according to the divinity that I heard from the Father, but in the law and in the prophets. He speaks in the person of the flesh in order to dispel the error. "I do not speak on my own, but what I have heard from the Father. But you speak what you have heard from your father the devil." And to show that when the devil speaks he works falsehood in some, he says, "When he tells a lie, he speaks from his own." "I do not speak from myself," but from the prophets and from the law, for this is truth. So just as the Savior dispels the suspicion and throws off the evil charge by saying, "I do not speak on my own," as the deceivers did, so too with the Spirit.

Now, I beg you, let us fix our minds on this. In the Savior's case, many false christs and false prophets appear. One man said, "I am he," and another, "I am he," as it is written: "Many will come in my name, saying, 'I am the Christ,' and they will lead many astray; but do not be led astray." The name of Christ was falsely supposed to belong to the deceivers. In the same way, many would pretend to have the Holy Spirit, which they did not have, and would speak. But in the first case the man appeared and said, "I am the Christ." In this case no one dared to say, "I am the Holy Spirit," for the Spirit did not come in a body but was present invisibly. He came upon Peter, he came upon Paul, and it was acknowledged that they had the Spirit of the Lord. Then Simon popped up and said, "I have the Spirit." No one could tell by looking who did not have the Spirit, who had an unclean spirit, or who had the Holy Spirit. If the Spirit were visible, an impostor could not have slipped in, since being recognized would have exposed him. Montanus came saying, "I have the Holy Spirit"; Manichaeus came saying, "I have the Holy Spirit." But it was not evident. So that people would not be deceived by the name, since the gift was going to come invisibly, he says: "When the Paraclete comes, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will remind you of my words and guide you into all the truth; for he will not speak on his own." If you see someone who says, "I have the Holy Spirit," and yet speaks not the things of the Gospel but his own, he is speaking on his own, and there is no Holy Spirit in him. He says of himself, "I do not speak on my own," to dispel the suspicion that he was a deceiver. In the same way he says of the Spirit, "He will not speak on his own," in order to separate error from truth and to show who have the Holy Spirit and who do not but pretend to have it. You have heard from me what I handed down. When the invisible Spirit comes, he will speak what is mine. If you see someone repeating the things of the Gospel, he truly has the Holy Spirit, for the Spirit comes to remind you of what I taught. So if anyone who claims to have the Spirit says something on his own and not from the Gospels, do not believe him. Keep in line with my teaching: "He will not speak on his own." Instead, the coming of the Spirit itself shows who has received the Holy Spirit and who has not: whoever repeats the things of Christ has the Holy Spirit. "For no one can say 'Jesus is Lord' except by the Holy Spirit." Mani came, truly a maniac, whose name fits his error, and he says: "I am the Paraclete whom the Savior promised to the apostles; I am the son of God." Where did you hear in the Gospel of Jesus Christ that the sun and the moon are creators? Where did Christ say that they draw up souls and carry them on high? Where have you read this? Because he does not say what is written but speaks on his own, it is clear that he does not have the Holy Spirit. "The Holy Spirit will not speak on his own, but whatever he hears he will declare to you"; that is, he will confirm what I have spoken. And see how wonderful this is. When the Savior came, he became the fulfillment of the law and the prophets; so too the Spirit is the fulfillment of the Gospel. When Christ came, he confirmed what came from the Father, what was said in the law and the prophets. That is why Paul says, "Christ is the fulfillment of the law." When the Holy Spirit came, he fulfilled what belongs to the Gospel. Christ fulfills whatever is in the law; the Spirit fulfills whatever is in Christ's teaching. This is not because the Father was incomplete. Rather, just as Christ appeared confirming what was the Father's, so the Holy Spirit appeared confirming what was the Son's. How do we know this? The Savior says to the disciples: "I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when the Holy Spirit comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his own." For he fulfills what is mine. The Son completes what is the Father's and does not speak on his own; the Spirit completes what is the Son's and does not speak on his own. But if you hear him say, "I will send you the Holy Spirit," do not take it as referring to the divinity, for God is not sent. These are names that signify the activity, names that are both hidden and shining: hidden as regards his dignity, shining to those who contemplate them. For example, anyone who sends someone sends him to places where he himself is not present. Suppose I am the one speaking from this seat. I cannot say to someone, "Come, I will send you here." That is not sending; it is seating someone beside me or having him stand beside me. But if God is everywhere ("For I fill heaven and earth," he says), where does he who is everywhere send anyone? "If I go up to heaven, you are there; if I go down to Hades, you are present; if I take my wings at dawn and settle at the farthest limits of the sea, even there your hand will guide me." Where, then, does God send? Or is it that he is everywhere but the one who is sent is not? "God sent his Son into the world." As though he were not present in the world? Yet the world comes from the Son. Did he come into the world, then, as though he had not been in the world before? Then how does John the evangelist say, "All things came into being through him; he was in the world, and the world came into being through him"? How, then, was he sent into the world? Again, if the one who was sent was sent, and the sender stayed above while the one sent was below, how could he say, "And the one who sent me is with me"?

Pay careful attention, I beg you, and make sure the argument is secure. For the heretic can say, "He is with me by his help," just as I too say, "God is with me." But he did not say it in that simple sense. What did he say? "The Father who dwells in me." If he was with him and dwelt in him, how did the one send or the other be sent? If they came, both came, and no one was sent. Or again, both remained. If the Father remained above, how does the Son say, "The Father is with me"? If the sender remained above, how does the one sent have the sender with him? For he said, "I am in the Father, and the Father is with me." How, then, was he sent who says, "The Father is in me"? And how, again, did the Father send? So when he says, "I will send you the Holy Spirit," he means the gift of the Spirit. And so that you may learn that the gift is sent but the Spirit is not, the Savior says to the apostles: "Stay in Jerusalem until you are clothed with power from on high, and you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you." The power supplied is one thing; the Spirit who supplies it is another. "For one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one individually as he wills." You cannot show that the Holy Spirit is sent by the Godhead as such. But if I show you the maker of heaven and earth being sent by the Holy Spirit, what will you do? Either deny Christ and erase the Scriptures, or, as a servant of the Scriptures, submit to the Scriptures. "And where," he asks, "is this said?" Listen to God speaking through the prophet Isaiah, the herald of true religion: "Listen to me, Jacob, and Israel whom I call: I am God, the first, and I am after these things, and besides me there is no God." Pay attention, for here at last is the point at issue. Who said these things, the Father or the Son? See how, in the form of a single rule, he proclaims the Trinity in veiled terms: "I am God, the first, and I am after these things, and besides me there is no God." Who is saying this? The Creator, for he adds, "With my hand I laid the foundation of the earth." See how the Creator speaks: "And my Spirit made the heavens firm. I gave orders to all the stars; I raised up a king in righteousness, and all my ways are straight." Having called himself Creator and maker of heaven and earth, he goes on to say: "From the beginning I have not spoken these things to you in secret, nor in a dark place." Having said that he laid the foundation of the earth and made the heavens, he continues: "When they came into being, I was there. And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit." You who made heaven and earth, who gave orders to the stars, who say, "The Lord has sent me, and his Spirit": he begot you according to the Godhead and sent you according to the flesh. The maker of heaven says, "The Lord has sent me, and his Spirit." The heretic takes the sending of the Spirit as an insult to the Spirit. The Father sent without moving from his place or moving the Son from his; the Son sent the Spirit without dividing him and without being divided. That is why Scripture says, "God poured out his Spirit," meaning the gift of the Holy Spirit. The Godhead is not poured out, but the gift is. So, to show that what is poured out is not the Holy Spirit but the grace of the divine Spirit, David says to Christ, "Grace is poured out on your lips." Grace is poured out, not the one who bestows the grace. If, then, equal honor is proclaimed, if "on his own" has been made clear, and if "he will take from what is mine" has been explained as drawing from a reservoir, let the heretics have no room or entry for their impiety. Honor the Holy Spirit whom you have received. I have often said that you have received something in exchange. Christ took from you what was fashioned from you, and he gave you his own Holy Spirit. He honored your nature by seating it at the right hand of the Father, and you have put his Spirit in the rank of a servant. This is what the saving law dictates, the prophets proclaim, the apostles decree, the martyrs confess and the faithful believe. The church agrees, the stubborn fight against it, the believer is fully assured, and Christ is glorified. For to him belong glory, honor and worship, together with the Father and the all-holy and life-giving Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
